Needs uninitialization/cleanup for the touch data.

Also you need to uninitialize the touch object into `WaylandThread::destroy`, like with the rest of the input objects (yes, this is annoying, I plan on removing this duplication)

This is a bit complicated to explain. I can give a hand if you need one.

Basically, the purpose of a "frame" event is to accumulate all data _before_ emitting events. This is to allow for composite data to be described predictably (e.g. from `shape` and `orientation`, which describe the same ellipse), along other things we can't really control.

We should strive to implement this properly to be as compliant to the Wayland specifications as possible, to avoid nasty surprises down the road.

Because of this, I advise to take the same approach as `wl_pointer::frame` and compare the data before/after.

This comparison is the reason behind the "buffer" concept, which as you can see with the pointer has a "buffer" and "committed" value.

For reference, [the spec says](https://wayland.app/protocols/wayland#wl_touch:event:frame):
> Indicates the end of a set of events that logically belong together. A client is expected to accumulate the data in all events within the frame before proceeding.

Hope that was clear, feel free to ask if you need anything :D

Oh that's interesting. I don't know much about touch screens as I don't have them, but does your touchscreen do that? Also, do you know if that's a common thing to do? We don't necessarily have to set a pressure.

Same to the above, is this a common thing to do? I'm not sure if I understand it correctly, as the tilt is meant for something like a drawing tablet, with the pen tilting perpendicularly to the surface in question.

The orientation value is related to a _rotation in the perpendicular axis_. In other words, this is rotating in the wrong way, I think.

Personally, while I appreciate the effort, I'd avoid emulating pressure & tilt as those are commonly related to drawing tablets (or at the very least a pen), more than plain touchscreens operated with fingers. I think that the only common touch screen with pressure sensitivity was on the iphone 6.

I'm not a huge data structure expert, but I think that the less-known `AHashMap` would be better suited for this case. It's more performant and very well suited for few keys (realistically we're not going to get more than 10 touchpoints at a time).

now, regarding that "frame" stuff: the pointer stuff has two `PointerData`, one with the committed data and one without. While you could do the same here, I think that this might make data comparison a lot more annoying.

Because of this, it might make more sense to move "buffering" to each touch point and iterate over them, I think.

My touchscreen also doesn't have the ability to detect touch pressure. As for the code for detecting touch pressure and pen tilt, I got it by copying answers from AI. I think it should be possible to delete this code, right?

Oh all right. Next time, please tell us what you couldn't test. In general, I recommend not writing code for features that you can't test or find somebody, as if there's any issue (e.g. crash), it will trigger only with people that have that feature.

Also, next time, please do disclose in advance what you used AI for. See [our guidelines](https://contributing.godotengine.org/en/latest/organization/general_rules_and_guidelines.html#ai-assisted-contributions) for the rationale.

Yes, you can entirely delete the emulation code, as I don't think that the shape data is enough for a good approximation.

Note: this is not how you iterate on a HashMap. This probably works because the index is _usually_ 0, 1, 2, 3... but [the spec](https://wayland.app/protocols/wayland#wl_touch:event:down) does not guarantee this:

> A new touch point has appeared on the surface. This touch point is assigned a unique ID. Future events from this touch point reference this ID. The ID ceases to be valid after a touch up event and **may** be reused in the future.

I actually asked in the Wayland chat to make sure, and that "may" (emphasis mine), along with other wording choices, make it perfectly valid for a compositor to use whatever number it thinks of.

To iterate properly on all elements of a HashMap, you can do this:
```suggestion
	for (KeyValue<int32_t, TouchPoint> &pair: bf.touchs) {
		TouchPoint &td = pair.value;
```

This code iterates through all entries in the map, and selects the value from them.
